titulo: Who Ruled Italy? 2,500 Years in 7 Parts
descricao_youtube: Kings, senators, emperors, popes, foreign crowns, a dictator, and finally the voters. The full story of who ruled the land we call Italy, from the Roman Republic in 509 BC to the Italian Republic of 1946, including how a pope ended up with his own country the size of a golf course. Every claim is sourced below.

intro.narracao: In two and a half thousand years, Italy was run by kings, senators, emperors, popes, foreign crowns and a dictator. Then its people voted for none of the above.

visual.cena: The channel mascot troll standing on a giant map of the Italian boot, juggling a Roman legionary helmet, a golden royal crown, a white papal tiara and a wooden ballot box, looking at the camera with a calm grin, sunny Mediterranean sky behind him

intro.narracao: This is the story of who ruled that boot-shaped peninsula, told in seven parts.

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 1: The Republic #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part two: Rome gets an emperor. Follow.

trechos.narracao: According to Roman tradition, in 509 BC the people of Rome threw out their last king and swore they would never have another one.

visual.cena: Roman citizens in togas cheering as they push a sulking king in a purple robe out through the city gates, his golden crown rolling on the road; the mascot troll, wearing a toga over his green suspenders, waves him goodbye with a smile

trechos.narracao: Instead they built a republic: two consuls elected for one year at a time, advised by a senate of rich families.
Over the next centuries, that one city conquered the whole peninsula, then Carthage, Greece and Spain.
But winning generals got rich and dangerous. In 49 BC, Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army and started a civil war.
He won and was named dictator for life. Weeks later, in 44 BC, senators stabbed him to death. The republic was already over.

fontes.afirmacao: Traditional founding of the Republic in 509 BC after the expulsion of Tarquin; consuls and senate; expansion across Italy and the Mediterranean; Caesar and the end of the Republic
Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC; appointed dictator perpetuo in early 44 BC; assassinated on 15 March 44 BC

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 2: The Emperors #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part three: Rome changes gods. Follow.

trechos.narracao: Caesar's adopted son Octavian won the next civil war, and in 27 BC the senate named him Augustus. He never once called himself king.

visual.cena: A young ruler in a laurel wreath politely refusing a golden crown offered by senators, while a huge ring of keys labeled with symbols of Rome hangs from his belt; the mascot troll, dressed as a senator, raises an eyebrow and nudges the senator next to him

trechos.narracao: He didn't need to. He controlled the army, the money and the elections, and the senate almost always agreed with him.
By 117 AD the empire stretched from Britain to Iraq, with Italy in the middle, paying almost no direct taxes.
Then the privilege faded. In 212 almost every free person became a Roman citizen, and in 330 the capital moved to Constantinople.
Rome was still famous, just no longer in charge. And the emperor who moved the capital had a new god.

fontes.afirmacao: Octavian became Augustus in 27 BC and ruled as princeps while keeping republican forms
Greatest extent under Trajan in 117 AD; Italy's privileged status; the Constitutio Antoniniana of 212
Constantinople dedicated as the new capital in 330

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 3: The Fall of Rome #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part four: the pope becomes a king. Follow.

trechos.narracao: In 312, before a battle outside Rome, Emperor Constantine had his soldiers mark a Christian symbol on their shields. He won.

visual.cena: Roman soldiers by a river at dawn painting a Christian chi-rho symbol on their red shields, while their emperor in purple watches the sky; the mascot troll, dressed as a legionary, carefully paints the symbol on his own shield with his tongue out in concentration

trechos.narracao: In 313 Christians could worship freely, and by 380 Christianity was the official religion of the whole empire.
Meanwhile the West was falling apart. In 410 the Visigoths sacked Rome, the first enemy to take it in eight hundred years.
In 476 a Germanic general, Odoacer, removed the last western emperor, a teenager, and didn't bother replacing him.

visual.texto_tela: 476: no more emperor in the West

trechos.narracao: Rome had no emperor anymore. But it still had a bishop, and the bishop of Rome was about to get much bigger.

fontes.afirmacao: Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 and the Christian symbol on the shields
Edict of Milan (313) granted religious tolerance
Edict of Thessalonica (380) made Nicene Christianity the state religion
Sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410, the first in about 800 years
Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 4: The Pope's Kingdom #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part five: a fake document. Follow.

trechos.narracao: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo the Third crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor. His biographer says Charlemagne didn't see it coming.

visual.cena: Inside a candlelit old basilica on Christmas Day, a pope in white places a golden crown on a big bearded king kneeling in prayer, who looks up startled; the mascot troll, dressed as a monk in a brown robe, holds a tall candle and grins at the camera

trechos.narracao: Why could a bishop crown emperors? After Rome fell, Goths, Byzantines and Lombards fought over Italy, and the popes needed a protector.
In 756 the Frankish king Pepin beat the Lombards and gave their lands in central Italy to the pope. The Papal States were born.
Now the pope was two things at once: head of the Western Church, and a king with land, taxes and armies.
To prove it was legitimate, popes pointed to an old document in which Emperor Constantine handed them the West. There was one problem.

fontes.afirmacao: Charlemagne crowned emperor by Leo III on Christmas Day 800; Einhard's claim that he would not have entered the church had he known
Lombard invasion of Italy and the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna
Donation of Pepin (756) as the legal basis of the Papal States
The Papal States as the pope's temporal realm in central Italy

capitulos.titulo: A Fake Document and a Broken Italy

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 5: The Fake Document #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part six: a thousand red shirts. Follow.

trechos.narracao: The document was fake. In 1440 a scholar, Lorenzo Valla, showed its Latin was centuries too young to be Constantine's.

visual.cena: A Renaissance scholar in a red cap at a cluttered desk points with a quill at a line in an old parchment, under a magnifying glass, while two shocked cardinals peek around a bookshelf; the mascot troll, dressed as the scholar's apprentice in a tunic and cap, holds a candle closer with a knowing look

trechos.narracao: The popes kept their lands anyway. Italy was not one country, but a patchwork of rival states.
Venice ruled the sea, Florence the banks, Milan had dukes, Naples had kings. They made the Renaissance, and kept fighting.
Divided and rich, Italy was easy prey: from 1494 France, Spain and Austria took turns ruling it.
When Napoleon fell in 1815, Europe handed Italy back to its old rulers. But many Italians now dreamed of one country.

fontes.afirmacao: Lorenzo Valla proved the Donation of Constantine a forgery in 1440 using linguistic evidence
The Donation of Constantine as an 8th-century forgery
The Italian Wars from 1494 and foreign domination of Italy
Napoleon annexed the Papal States in 1809; the Congress of Vienna restored the old states in 1815

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 6: Italy Is Born #Shorts
short.pergunta: Part seven: a dictator and a vote. Follow.

trechos.narracao: In May 1860, about a thousand volunteers in red shirts, led by Giuseppe Garibaldi, landed in Sicily and conquered a whole kingdom.

visual.cena: About a thousand volunteers in bright red shirts leaping off two old steamships onto a sunny Sicilian beach, cheering and waving the Italian tricolor; the mascot troll in a red shirt over his green suspenders runs ahead holding the flag

trechos.narracao: Garibaldi handed it to King Victor Emmanuel the Second, and in 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was declared.

visual.busca: Meeting of Teano Garibaldi Victor Emmanuel

trechos.narracao: Except Rome. The French protected the pope until 1870, when they left to fight Prussia and Italian soldiers broke through Rome's walls.
Pope Pius the Ninth shut himself inside the Vatican and called himself a prisoner. His successors did the same for fifty-nine years.
Italy had a king, a parliament and Rome as its capital. Peace with the pope would come from a very unlikely man.

fontes.afirmacao: Expedition of the Thousand landed at Marsala in May 1860 and conquered the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
Proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861; Venice in 1866
Capture of Rome on 20 September 1870 after French troops withdrew for the Franco-Prussian War
Popes considered themselves prisoners in the Vatican from 1870 to 1929

capitulos.titulo: A Dictator, a War and a Vote

short.titulo: Who Ruled Italy? Part 7: Italians Fire the King #Shorts
short.abertura: Who ruled Italy? Part seven, the finale.
short.pergunta: Which country should I do next?

trechos.narracao: On June 2, 1946, Italians voted on their king. Fifty-four percent chose a republic, and the king left for exile.

visual.cena: Italian men and women in 1940s clothes lining up at a polling station; a woman proudly drops her ballot into a wooden box, while in the background a sad king in uniform carries his suitcases toward a waiting car; the mascot troll in a 1940s suit and hat holds his own ballot and tips his hat

trechos.narracao: Why? In 1922 the king had let Benito Mussolini's fascists take power, and Italy became a dictatorship.
Mussolini made peace with the pope: the 1929 Lateran Treaty created Vatican City, the smallest country on Earth.
Then he joined Hitler in World War Two. Italy was invaded and split in two, and in 1945 partisans executed him.
So after twenty-five centuries, Italy ended up where Rome began in 509 BC: a republic that had just thrown out its king.

fontes.afirmacao: 2 June 1946 institutional referendum: about 54.3% for the republic; Umberto II left for exile in Portugal
March on Rome in October 1922; the king appointed Mussolini prime minister
The 1929 Lateran Treaty created Vatican City, about 44 hectares
Italy in the Second World War, the 1943 armistice and the death of Mussolini in April 1945

outro.narracao: Kings, consuls, emperors, popes, foreign crowns, a dictator and finally the voters. Italy has tried almost every way to run a country, and it remembers all of them.

alertas: Formato novo (série em Partes, formato 3): cada capítulo é uma Parte inteira que vira um Short de até 60 s; a fala 'pergunta' faz o gancho para a Parte seguinte.
Tom neutro e leve, sem Troll-o-meter; o Snorri aparece dentro de cada cena vestido de acordo com a época.
Parte 1: 509 a.C. e a expulsão de Tarquínio são a data e o relato tradicionais romanos; o roteiro diz 'according to Roman tradition'.
Parte 2: 'quase nenhum imposto direto' na Itália é simplificação (a Itália ficou isenta do tributum por muito tempo).
Parte 3: a fala 'teenager' para Rômulo Augústulo segue a estimativa usual (~16 anos).
Parte 4: a surpresa de Carlos Magno vem do biógrafo dele, Einhard; o roteiro diz 'his biographer claims'. A fala 'handed the West' resume a Doação de Constantino.
Parte 5: Valla é datado em 1440 na maioria das fontes (há quem diga 1439).
Parte 7: 54,3% é o resultado oficial; a execução de Mussolini é contada de forma factual e sem imagem.
